meta.blurb: Joy is eight and runs everywhere for fun. Her father Sam, forty-two, cannot sprint a few steps without gasping. With a patient coach and a walk-run plan, he starts slowly, with one small town fun run in sight.
meta.bible: Sam: a forty-two-year-old office worker who has not run since school, cheerful and a little stubborn. Joy: his eight-year-old daughter, who runs everywhere for fun. Ana: a volunteer running coach in her fifties, calm and funny, who leads a Saturday morning beginners group in Elm Park. Maria: a sixty-eight-year-old club runner and a friend of Ana. The story lasts twelve weeks and ends with a fun run of five kilometres in the town. Key ideas: walk-run, the talk test, easy pace, short quick steps, rest days, strength work, doing too much too soon, runner's high, warm-up, taper. The science is real and hedged: scientists think humans may be well built for long-distance running but this is debated; research on shoes, stretching and the ten percent rule is mixed; no invented numbers or studies. Anyone with a health condition should speak to a doctor before starting. Voice: warm, encouraging, practical, never pushy. Leila: Sam's wife and Joy's mother, kind and funny, who circles the Saturdays on the fridge calendar. Dev: Sam's colleague at the office, who laughs at first and later comes to cheer. Dr Rao: Sam's doctor. Nadia: a shy young accountant in the beginners group. Frank: a retired bus driver in the group, cheerful and full of jokes. Mr Okafor: Sam's neighbour at number twelve. Biscuit: Mr Okafor's small round dog. Maria also leads the Tuesday evening club run. Fixed facts: the Saturday group meets at nine in Elm Park; the first Saturday is walking and talking, the jogging begins on the second; the walk-run plan is one minute of jogging and two of walking; the knee ache comes in week three and Sam rests for about a week; Sam first runs twenty minutes without stopping in week eight, thirty minutes in week ten; the taper is in week eleven; the Elm Town Fun Run is five kilometres, about three miles, through two parks, along the riverbank and under the old stone bridge; Joy waits at the finish with a banner that says Go Dad; Dev's sign says Next year, me. Achilles tendon, Elm Town. This book is general information and is not medical advice.
chapters: A Yellow Jacket at the Gate
Rain, Heat and a Runaway Dog

beats.scene: Sam bends over, out of breath, while his daughter runs on with a ball
beats.summary: Sam is out of breath after a short sprint, while his daughter Joy runs on easily.

beats.scene: Joy runs in circles across the grass, arms wide and laughing
beats.summary: Joy runs for no reason except joy, and Sam wonders what she knows that he has forgotten.

beats.scene: Sam walks home slowly beside Joy, who skips along and chatters
beats.summary: On the walk home Joy asks why Dad always stops, and Sam has no good answer.

beats.scene: Leila hands Sam a mug of tea in the kitchen while he sighs
beats.summary: At home Sam tells his wife Leila what happened, and she gently reminds him that he used to run.

beats.scene: Sam finds a small old school running medal in a drawer
beats.summary: Sam finds an old school running medal in a drawer and remembers that he once loved to run.

beats.scene: A boy races his friends across a school playground at lunchtime
beats.summary: Sam remembers racing his friends at lunchtime and the joy of being fast.

beats.scene: Sam sits at an office desk, staring at a screen beside a cold cup
beats.summary: Sam sees that his days are now made of chairs: the car, the desk and the sofa.

beats.scene: Sam sits on the sofa with a phone full of running advice
beats.summary: Sam searches online for how to start and is bewildered by advice that contradicts itself.

beats.scene: A paper notice on a park gate says beginners are welcome on Saturdays
beats.summary: Sam notices a sign for a free Saturday beginners group in Elm Park, led by a volunteer coach.

beats.scene: Sam sits in a doctor's room while Dr Rao listens to his chest
beats.summary: Sam visits Dr Rao, who tells him that a gentle start is a good way to begin.

beats.scene: Joy ties the laces of a pair of old trainers by the front door
beats.summary: On Friday night Sam puts his old trainers by the door and Joy ties the laces in a double knot.

beats.scene: Sam stands alone at the park gate with his hands in his pockets
beats.summary: On Saturday morning Sam almost turns back at the park gate, afraid that he will look foolish.

beats.scene: A woman in a bright yellow jacket greets a small group in a park
beats.summary: Sam joins the Saturday beginners group in Elm Park and meets the coach, Ana.

beats.scene: Five nervous strangers stand in a circle on the grass, saying their names
beats.summary: The group introduces itself: Nadia is shy, and Frank, a retired bus driver, is a beginner too.

beats.scene: Ana laughs and waves a hand across the group of nervous beginners
beats.summary: Ana says that nobody is too old, too heavy or too slow, and that the slowest person sets the pace.

beats.scene: Ana raises a hand and points to a health sign beside the group
beats.summary: Ana says that anyone with a health condition should talk to a doctor before starting to run.

beats.scene: Ana holds up three fingers beside a whiteboard with three short rules
beats.summary: Ana gives three rules: go slowly, be kind to yourself, and stop while you could still do more.

beats.scene: The group sits on the grass while Ana points at each person in turn
beats.summary: Ana asks why each person wants to run, and Sam says he wants to keep up with his daughter.

beats.scene: The group walks past a notice board with a poster for a fun run
beats.summary: On a gentle lap of the park the group sees a poster for the Elm Town Fun Run, five kilometres, twelve weeks away.

beats.scene: Ana sits the group on the grass and draws a big question mark
beats.summary: After the lap, Ana asks the group a question: are human beings built to run?

beats.scene: Ana draws a tall running figure with long legs on a whiteboard
beats.summary: Ana says scientists think the human body may be well built for running long distances.

beats.scene: A dog, a horse and a person race, the person far behind
beats.summary: Humans are poor sprinters next to dogs, horses and cheetahs, but may be good at lasting a long time.

beats.scene: A sweating runner on a hot day beside a panting dog in the shade
beats.summary: Humans cool down by sweating over most of the skin, which may help them keep going in the heat.

beats.scene: A runner in strong sun wipes a sweating forehead beside a shady tree
beats.summary: Ana warns that the body's cooling has limits, and runners should slow down on hot days.

beats.scene: A drawing of a foot and heel with a spring beside it
beats.summary: The Achilles tendon and the arch of the foot work like springs that return energy with each step.

beats.scene: A human foot with short toes drawn beside the long-toed foot of an ape
beats.summary: Long legs and short toes may help people run, though scientists still discuss how much each matters.

beats.scene: A runner seen from behind with strong leg muscles and an upright back
beats.summary: Strong buttock muscles help keep the upper body steady and upright while running.

beats.scene: A runner with a steady head and arms swinging against the legs
beats.summary: The arms swing against the legs to keep the body balanced, and a neck ligament may steady the head.

beats.scene: Early hunters walk across a hot plain after a distant antelope
beats.summary: Some scientists suggest early humans chased animals until they were exhausted, but this is debated.

beats.scene: The group stands in a circle in the park while Ana waves her arms
beats.summary: Ana says that whatever the past was, a body trained gently can learn to run, and starting small is the key.

beats.scene: Ana holds up a plain trainer and points to the space at its toe
beats.summary: Ana says a comfortable, well-fitting shoe is enough, and the research on expensive shoes is mixed.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy stand before a wall of colourful trainers in a busy shop
beats.summary: Sam takes Joy to a sports shop, where a wall of trainers overwhelms him until an assistant helps.

beats.scene: Sam presses his thumb against the toe of a trainer on his foot
beats.summary: Sam tries shoes on, leaves a thumb's width in front of the toes, and jogs a few steps in the shop.

beats.scene: Soft socks and a plaster beside a sore heel on a bench
beats.summary: Soft, dry socks and well-fitting shoes help prevent blisters, and new shoes should be worn in gently.

beats.scene: A pair of bare feet running on a grassy path at the park edge
beats.summary: Some people like barefoot running, but the science is not settled and anyone trying it should go very slowly.

beats.scene: A runner's feet on grass, pavement and a muddy trail
beats.summary: Different surfaces feel different: grass is softer, pavement is firmer, and variety is good for the body.

beats.scene: Sam lays a plain T-shirt, shorts and a light jacket on the bed
beats.summary: Beginners do not need special clothes: a light, comfortable outfit is enough.

beats.scene: Sam walks briskly beside a river in the evening light in new shoes
beats.summary: Sam does his homework of three brisk walks in the week, and by the third he is enjoying them.

beats.scene: A paper calendar on a fridge with Saturdays circled in green pen
beats.summary: Leila circles the twelve Saturdays on the family calendar, and the household joins Sam's plan.

beats.scene: Sam lies awake in bed with new shoes beside him and the moon outside
beats.summary: On Friday night Sam lies awake, nervous about his first run, and Leila reminds him the hardest part is done.

beats.scene: The group lines up on the park path while Ana holds a stopwatch
beats.summary: On the second Saturday Ana explains the walk-run plan: one minute of gentle jogging, then two minutes of walking.

beats.scene: The group lines up along the path as Ana lifts a silver whistle
beats.summary: Before the first jog Ana tells everyone to start slower than they think they should, and Sam ignores her.

beats.scene: Sam leans forward with a red face and open mouth while others pass calmly
beats.summary: Sam starts too fast and gasps, and Ana tells him to go slower than he thinks he should.

beats.scene: Sam and Nadia walk side by side, red in the face and laughing
beats.summary: In the first walking break Sam and Nadia compare notes and find that they both thought everyone else was finding it easy.

beats.scene: Frank hums and swings his arms as the group jogs in a line
beats.summary: They repeat the pattern again and again, and Frank hums an old song to keep the rhythm.

beats.scene: Two runners chat while jogging side by side along a tree-lined path
beats.summary: The talk test: you should be able to speak in short sentences while you run, and that tells you your pace is right.

beats.scene: Sam jogs slowly while a brisk walker nearly keeps pace beside him
beats.summary: Sam's slow jogging is barely faster than walking, and Ana says that this is exactly the right speed.

beats.scene: A runner breathes out in a cold morning, with a small cloud of breath
beats.summary: There is no special breathing method; breathe in whatever way feels natural, through the nose, the mouth or both.

beats.scene: Sam holds his side and winces while Ana jogs beside him
beats.summary: Sam gets a stitch; scientists are not sure what causes it, and slowing down and breathing out usually helps.

beats.scene: A relaxed runner stands tall with eyes on the horizon and loose shoulders
beats.summary: Good posture means standing tall, relaxing the shoulders and looking ahead rather than down.

beats.scene: Feet landing close under a runner's body, with short quick steps
beats.summary: Short, quick steps that land under the body are usually easier on the legs than long, reaching strides.

beats.scene: Ana claps a steady rhythm while the group tries to match their steps
beats.summary: Ana claps a steady rhythm and the group matches their steps to it, which makes their steps lighter and quicker.

beats.scene: A runner's foot landing flat on the path beside two other styles
beats.summary: Runners land on the heel, the middle or the front of the foot, and the research does not show that one way is best.

beats.scene: A runner's arms swing gently with relaxed loose hands
beats.summary: The arms should swing loosely, with relaxed hands, as if holding a bag of crisps without crushing it.

beats.scene: A runner with a clenched jaw relaxes it into a gentle smile
beats.summary: Ana tells the group to relax the face and jaw, and Sam finds that a loose jaw makes the whole body looser.

beats.scene: A runner's long shadow on the path, with a bouncing head and arms
beats.summary: Sam sees his running shadow on the path and laughs, because he looks like a real runner.

beats.scene: The group walks slowly in a circle, arms loose, breathing deeply
beats.summary: After the last jog the group walks to cool down, and Sam realises that twenty minutes have gone by.

beats.scene: Ana hands Sam a small notebook and a pencil on a park bench
beats.summary: Ana suggests keeping a short log: one line after each run about how it felt, not times.

beats.scene: Joy holds the front door open as a tired Sam limps in grinning
beats.summary: At home Joy asks whether her father really ran, and Sam says he ran in little pieces, which she says still count.

beats.scene: Joy bounces across the garden on tiptoe while Sam copies her
beats.summary: In the garden Joy shows her father how to run like a kid: bouncy, light and without a care.

beats.scene: Sam walks stiffly down the stairs while holding the handrail and wincing
beats.summary: Mild muscle soreness after a first run is normal, but sharp pain is a signal to stop.

beats.scene: Sam walks gently round the block with a stiff, careful stride
beats.summary: Gentle movement often eases stiff muscles, so Sam goes for a slow walk on Sunday afternoon.

beats.scene: Sam rests on a sofa with his feet up while Joy brings water
beats.summary: Sam rests on the sofa while Joy plays nurse and Leila teases him gently.

beats.scene: Sam rests with his feet up while his body grows stronger
beats.summary: Rest days matter, because the body grows stronger during rest; beginners should run every other day.

beats.scene: Sam stares at his running shoes by the door on a rest day
beats.summary: Sam is impatient on a rest day, but he remembers Ana's rule to stop while he still wants more.

beats.scene: Dev leans on Sam's office desk, grinning, as Sam stands up stiffly
beats.summary: At work Dev laughs at Sam's stiff walk, then admits that he has always wanted to run but could never do it.

beats.scene: Sam sets a phone timer on the kitchen table beside his running shoes
beats.summary: On Tuesday Sam plans his first run alone, with a phone timer that beeps for the jogs and walks.

beats.scene: Sam jogs along his street at dusk as a neighbour waves
beats.summary: Sam runs on his own street at dusk, and his neighbour Mr Okafor and his dog Biscuit cheer him on.

beats.scene: Sam writes a line in a small notebook at the kitchen table
beats.summary: After his first solo run Sam writes a line in his notebook and ticks the day on the fridge calendar.

beats.scene: Joy peeps round the kitchen door in muddy trainers, asking to come
beats.summary: Joy asks if she can run with him on Thursday, and Sam says yes.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy run side by side along the path with Joy skipping ahead
beats.summary: In the second week Joy joins Sam, and he sees how children treat running as a game.

beats.scene: Ana gives Joy a high five in front of the group in the park
beats.summary: Ana welcomes Joy to the Saturday group and says that children are the best teachers of running.

beats.scene: Sam, red in the face, glances sideways at Joy, who is hardly breathing
beats.summary: Sam is a little jealous of how easy running is for Joy, and he is also very proud.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy race to a lamp post, then walk laughing
beats.summary: Playing with speed, such as racing to a lamp post, makes training fun and teaches the body to change pace.

beats.scene: Sam points to a big oak tree far ahead and Joy grins
beats.summary: Sam invents his own game: jog to the next tree, walk to the one after, and Joy joins in.

beats.scene: Joy and Sam jog like robots on the path, with stiff arms
beats.summary: Joy makes up new games every few minutes: robots, ducks and very slow cheetahs.

beats.scene: Joy puts a hand flat on her chest and Sam crouches to listen
beats.summary: Joy asks why her heart goes boom when she runs, and Sam promises they will find out together.

beats.scene: Joy and Sam jog side by side at the same slow pace, smiling
beats.summary: Joy asks why Sam goes so slowly, and he says that slow is the point, so she becomes his pace-keeper.

beats.scene: Frank shows Joy how to whistle with a blade of grass
beats.summary: Frank, the retired bus driver, becomes friends with Joy and teaches her to whistle with a blade of grass.

beats.scene: The group sits on the grass with tea and a tin of biscuits
beats.summary: After the session the group sits together with tea and biscuits, and Sam feels that he belongs.

beats.scene: A runner drinks from a small bottle on a park bench in the sun
beats.summary: For short runs most people only need to drink when thirsty; there is no need to force down large amounts.

beats.scene: Sam sips a glass of water and a mug of tea after a run
beats.summary: Ordinary water is fine for short runs; there is no need for special sports drinks.

beats.scene: A bowl of porridge and a banana on a table in the morning light
beats.summary: Normal meals are enough for beginners; a small snack can help, but a big meal just before running is a bad idea.

beats.scene: Sam watches the kitchen clock beside a half-eaten sandwich
beats.summary: Sam learns to leave a gap between eating and running: a couple of hours after a big meal, or just a light snack.

beats.scene: Ana shakes her head at a calorie chart pinned to the notice board
beats.summary: Ana says there is no diet talk in her group, and running is not a punishment for eating.

beats.scene: Nadia talks quietly to Ana on a bench while the others stretch
beats.summary: Nadia admits that she is afraid of being judged, and Ana tells her that nobody is measuring bodies.

beats.scene: A family dinner of rice, beans and vegetables on the kitchen table
beats.summary: Sam is hungrier than before, and Leila cooks big, simple family meals; Joy says he eats like a horse.

beats.scene: Dev holds out a box of doughnuts across a busy office desk
beats.summary: Dev offers Sam a doughnut, and Sam takes one without guilt, because a treat is part of a happy life.

beats.scene: Joy paints stars and a rocket on Sam's plain water bottle
beats.summary: Joy decorates Sam's water bottle, and it becomes his lucky bottle.

beats.scene: Sam jogs briskly along the path, smiling, with a spring in his step
beats.summary: By the third week Sam feels strong and eager, and begins to think that the plan is too easy.

beats.scene: Sam jogs on a wet pavement at dusk with long determined strides
beats.summary: Sam decides to add extra runs on his own and to run faster than the plan says.

beats.scene: Sam checks his stopwatch and wipes his face with the back of a hand
beats.summary: Sam runs three days in a row, longer and faster each time, and feels like a champion.

beats.scene: Sam rubs his sore knee, sitting on a bench beside the path
beats.summary: In week three Sam's knee starts to ache, and Ana tells him to stop, rest and see a doctor or physiotherapist if it persists.

beats.scene: Ana crouches beside Sam on a bench, listening with a serious face
beats.summary: Ana asks what Sam did during the week, and he admits the extra runs; she says she is a coach, not a doctor.

beats.scene: Joy draws a get-well card with a big smiling knee on it
beats.summary: Sam is gloomy and frustrated, but Joy cheers him up with a get-well drawing.

beats.scene: Dr Rao presses gently on Sam's knee as he sits on the couch
beats.summary: Dr Rao examines the knee and says that in his case a few days of rest and a slow return should be enough.

beats.scene: Sam does a squat in the living room while Joy counts and copies him
beats.summary: Simple strength exercises such as squats, calf raises and planks twice a week may help runners avoid injuries.

beats.scene: Ana sits beside Sam on a bench and shows him a scar
beats.summary: Ana tells Sam that she once hurt herself by training too hard, and that setbacks happen to everyone.

beats.scene: A line drawing of a steadily rising staircase beside a runner's feet
beats.summary: Most running injuries come from doing too much too soon; the ten percent rule is only a rough guide.

beats.scene: Sam jogs gently for one minute, then walks, with a careful smile
beats.summary: After a week of rest Sam restarts at an easier stage of the plan, and the knee stays quiet.

beats.scene: Sam rises onto his toes at the kitchen sink while the kettle boils
beats.summary: Calf raises: Sam does them while the kettle boils, and the muscles at the back of his legs wake up.

beats.scene: Sam holds a plank on the living room floor with Joy beside him
beats.summary: The plank: Sam holds his body in a straight line for a short time, and Joy counts the seconds.

beats.scene: Sam balances on one leg while brushing his teeth at the mirror
beats.summary: Balancing on one leg trains the small muscles around the ankle and hip; Sam practises while brushing his teeth.

beats.scene: Sam lies on his back with knees bent and lifts his hips
beats.summary: The bridge is a simple exercise that strengthens the buttocks and the backs of the legs.

beats.scene: Leila squats beside Sam and Joy on the living room carpet
beats.summary: Leila joins in, and the whole family does the exercises together on Sunday evenings.

beats.scene: A drawing of leg muscles and tendons carrying a runner over a hill
beats.summary: Strong muscles and tendons share the load of running, and strength work may lower the risk of injury, though nothing can promise safety.

beats.scene: Sam and Leila walk by the river at sunset, hand in hand
beats.summary: On his rest days Sam takes gentle evening walks with Leila and notices things he missed when rushing.

beats.scene: Ana leads the group in brisk walking and easy leg swings
beats.summary: A warm-up of brisk walking and easy movements is a good start; the evidence for stretching before a run is mixed.

beats.scene: A runner walks slowly with hands on hips, cooling down after a run
beats.summary: After a run the group walks to cool down, and stretching is fine if it feels good, though the evidence is mixed.

beats.scene: Sam draws a green tick beside the fourth circled Saturday on the calendar
beats.summary: At the end of week four Sam ticks another Saturday and realises he has been running for a month.

beats.scene: Sam goes to bed early, and the moon shines through the window
beats.summary: Good sleep helps the body recover from running, and tired legs often need more sleep, not more miles.

beats.scene: Sam's head droops over his desk after a bad night
beats.summary: After a bad night Sam feels heavy and tired, so he chooses an early night over a run.

beats.scene: A dark bedroom with an alarm clock, a book and a glass of water
beats.summary: Ana suggests simple habits for sleep: regular times, a dark and quiet room, and less phone before bed.

beats.scene: A heart drawn inside a runner's chest with arrows showing blood moving
beats.summary: Ana explains that the heart is a muscle that regular running trains, so it pumps more blood with each beat.

beats.scene: Sam and Joy press two fingers to their wrists and count
beats.summary: Sam shows Joy how to find her pulse, and they discover that a child's heart beats faster than a grown-up's.

beats.scene: A runner stops and puts a hand on the chest beside a bench
beats.summary: A pounding heart is normal in running, but chest pain, dizziness or fainting mean stop and get medical help.

beats.scene: A strong bone and joint drawn with small arrows showing gentle pressure
beats.summary: Running puts gentle load on bones and joints, which can make bones stronger; studies have generally not found that recreational running wears out knees.

beats.scene: A drawing of a muscle taking in air with tiny arrows
beats.summary: Training helps the muscles to use oxygen better, though the lungs themselves change little.

beats.scene: Sam climbs office stairs while a surprised colleague watches
beats.summary: At work Sam climbs three flights of stairs without gasping and is quietly delighted.

beats.scene: Dev watches Sam walk past and holds up a hand for a high five
beats.summary: Dev notices the change in Sam and asks how he began; Sam says it started with a single minute.

beats.scene: A smiling runner at sunrise with arms spread wide on a hill
beats.summary: Some runners feel a happy lift called runner's high, but scientists are still unsure why, and not everyone feels it.

beats.scene: Joy jumps as high as she can beside Sam on the path
beats.summary: Joy asks what a runner's high is, and Sam explains that it is a happy feeling that does not come every time.

beats.scene: A drawing of a brain with tiny stars and question marks
beats.summary: Scientists once credited endorphins for the runner's high, newer research suggests other chemicals may matter too, and the question is open.

beats.scene: Sam walks in the park at sunrise with a lighter, calmer face
beats.summary: Many people say running clears the head, but it is not a treatment, and anyone with a long-lasting low mood should talk to a doctor.

beats.scene: Rain falls on an empty park path while Sam looks out of a window
beats.summary: On a rainy day without motivation Ana advises making the task small: put on the shoes and go out for ten minutes.

beats.scene: The group stands in the park in bright rain jackets, dripping and laughing
beats.summary: In the rain nearly the whole group turns up, and they agree that the hardest part was leaving the house.

beats.scene: Running shoes and a water bottle wait on a shelf by the front door
beats.summary: Ana says habits are built by making them easy: shoes by the door and the same days every week.

beats.scene: Sam sits at his office desk, watching the clock as it grows dark
beats.summary: Work runs late and Sam misses a run; Ana says a missed run is no failure and the next one is what matters.

beats.scene: Nadia looks at her phone on a bench, her shoes still in a bag
beats.summary: Nadia misses two Saturdays and nearly gives up, so Sam sends her a message saying that he will wait for her.

beats.scene: Nadia arrives at the park gate with a shy smile as the group claps
beats.summary: Nadia comes back on Saturday, and the group claps; she says that Sam's message made her put her shoes on.

beats.scene: A runner in a bright jacket runs through rain, sun and snow
beats.summary: Ana says the right clothes make every season easier: thin layers, slower runs in the heat, and bright colours in poor light.

beats.scene: The group jogs gently under a pink evening sky on a hot day
beats.summary: On a hot day Ana moves the session to the cool of the evening, and everyone runs slowly with a hat and water.

beats.scene: A runner in gloves and a woolly hat breathes out steam in frost
beats.summary: On a cold morning Ana advises a hat, gloves and a longer warm-up, because the first few minutes are the hardest.

beats.scene: A runner in a reflective vest on a dark pavement under a street lamp
beats.summary: As the evenings darken Sam buys a bright reflective vest so that drivers can see him from far away.

beats.scene: A runner on a pavement faces oncoming traffic with a phone in a pocket
beats.summary: Safety: run facing traffic, tell someone where you are going, carry a phone, and take care with headphones.

beats.scene: Sam writes his name and a phone number on a small card
beats.summary: Sam carries a card with his name and Leila's number, and tells her which way he is going and when he will be back.

beats.scene: Sam takes out one earbud as a bicycle bell rings behind him
beats.summary: Sam tries running with headphones, and when a bicycle bell startles him he decides to keep the volume low.

beats.scene: A small round dog chases Sam along a pavement with its lead trailing
beats.summary: Biscuit slips his lead and chases Sam, and Sam stays calm, slows to a walk and lets the dog lose interest.

beats.scene: A well-lit street with a lamp post and a runner on the pavement
beats.summary: At night Sam chooses well-lit, busy streets, and runs with someone from the group whenever he can.

beats.scene: A runner in a cap with sun cream on his nose
beats.summary: On bright days Sam wears a cap and sun cream, because the sun can burn even on cool days.

beats.scene: Sam jogs beside Maria, a smiling woman with grey hair, among other runners
beats.summary: Running with others makes it more fun, and Sam meets Maria, a sixty-eight-year-old club runner.

beats.scene: Maria shows an old photograph of a younger runner at a starting line
beats.summary: Maria tells Sam that she began running at thirty-eight, after years of thinking she was not a runner.

beats.scene: Maria jogs gently beside Sam, talking and smiling
beats.summary: Maria says that older bodies may need more time to recover, so she rests more and keeps up her strength exercises.

beats.scene: A friendly mix of runners meets under a lamp post on a Tuesday evening
beats.summary: Maria invites Sam to her club's easy Tuesday evening run, which welcomes every speed.

beats.scene: Two runners chat side by side while the sun sets behind trees
beats.summary: Running with a friend makes the minutes disappear, and Sam runs for a quarter of an hour without checking his watch.

beats.scene: Maria claps beside a finish line for runners who come in last
beats.summary: Maria says she has never won a race, but finishing is its own victory, and she is always glad she went.

beats.scene: Sam and Maria jog along a narrow path through a golden wood
beats.summary: On the club route Sam runs through an old wood that he never knew was there, so close to home.

beats.scene: A group of runners walks up a green hill and runs down it again
beats.summary: On hills, walk the steep parts with short steps and take care going downhill.

beats.scene: Maria runs down a long hill with short steps and loose arms
beats.summary: Maria shows Sam how she runs downhill: short quick steps, slightly bent knees, loose arms and eyes ahead.

beats.scene: Joy stands on top of a grassy hill with her arms raised
beats.summary: Sam and Joy climb the hill together, and from the top they look down on the whole town.

beats.scene: Ana stands with a stopwatch on a park bench as the group gathers
beats.summary: In week eight Ana announces a test: to jog for twenty minutes without a walking break, at a gentle pace.

beats.scene: Sam looks at the path stretching ahead, taking a deep breath
beats.summary: Sam is nervous, and Ana reminds him of the talk test and tells him to start slower than he thinks he should.

beats.scene: The group sets off along the path in a loose, chatting line
beats.summary: In the first five minutes the group settles into an easy rhythm, and Sam is surprised at how normal it feels.

B1B2: Sam is forty-two, and he has just run twenty steps after a football. He is gasping for air, while his daughter Joy is still racing happily across the grass.
Joy does not run to burn calories or to win a medal. She runs because it feels good, and she cannot imagine a reason not to.
On the way home, Joy asks why Sam always stops when they play. He laughs it off, but he knows that the true answer is not a funny one.
At home, Sam tells his wife Leila about the football and the twenty steps. She hands him a mug of tea and reminds him that he used to be quick.
That evening, Sam finds a small medal at the back of a drawer. It is from a school race, and it is the first time in years that he has thought about it.
He remembers the lunchtime races across the playground, with his friends shouting behind him. Being fast had felt like flying, and he had never stopped to ask why he gave it up.
Now his days are made of chairs: the car seat, the office desk and the sofa at night. He cannot remember the last time his heart beat fast for any good reason.
Sam searches online for ways to start running, and he finds a thousand opinions. Every page seems to disagree about shoes, plans and diets, so he ends up more confused than before.
On his way to work, Sam notices a small sign on the gate of Elm Park. It says that a free beginners group meets every Saturday morning, and that everyone is welcome.
Before he does anything, Sam makes an appointment with his doctor, Dr Rao. She asks careful questions and tells him that a gentle start is the right way to begin.
On Friday night, Sam puts his old trainers by the front door. Joy ties the laces in a double knot and says that now he has no excuse.
On Saturday morning, Sam stands at the gate of Elm Park with his heart pounding. He is not sure whether it is fear or the walk, and he almost turns around.
A cheerful woman in a bright yellow jacket waves him over and says her name is Ana. She has been a volunteer coach for many years, and she greets every newcomer as if they were an old friend.
Around the circle, everyone says a name and a reason for being there. Nadia is shy and a little afraid, while Frank, a retired bus driver, jokes that his doctor told him to move.
Ana tells the group that nobody is too old, too heavy or too slow. The rule is simple: the slowest person sets the pace, and everyone stays together.
Ana points at a small sign on the table about health. She says that anyone with a medical condition should speak to a doctor before they start to run.
Ana writes three rules on her whiteboard: go slowly, be kind, and finish with energy left. She says that a good session leaves you feeling that you could have done a little more.
Ana asks each person why they want to run, and the answers are very different. When it is his turn, Sam says quietly that he wants to keep up with his daughter.
On their gentle lap of the park, the group stops beside a poster for the Elm Town Fun Run. It is five kilometres, twelve weeks away, and Ana says that everyone here can be ready.
After the lap, Ana sits everyone down on the grass and draws a big question mark on her whiteboard. She asks the group something that nobody has ever asked Sam before: are human beings built to run?
Ana draws a tall figure with long legs and says that many scientists think our bodies may be built for running. She stresses that they are not certain, and that the idea is still discussed.
Ana is honest about our weakness: over a short distance, a dog, a horse or a cheetah would leave any person far behind. Our strength, she says, may lie in lasting for a long time instead.
Many animals cool down by panting, but people sweat across most of their skin. This may help us keep going on a hot day, long after other animals have to stop.
Ana adds a warning, because the body's cooling system has its limits. On a very hot or humid day, even the best runner should slow down, find shade and drink when thirsty.
Ana draws a heel and a foot, and next to them a spring. The Achilles tendon and the arch of the foot act like springs, giving back energy with every step.
Compared with our closest animal relatives, our legs are long and our toes are short. Some scientists think this helps with running, but nobody knows exactly how much.
One of the biggest muscles in the body sits in the buttock and works hard when we run. It helps to keep the upper body steady and upright with every stride.
When we run, our arms swing in the opposite direction to our legs, which keeps the body balanced. Some scientists also think a strong band in the neck helps to hold the head steady.
Some scientists suggest that early humans hunted by following an animal for hours until it was too tired to run. Others doubt this, and the question is still debated among experts.
Ana says that you do not have to believe any theory about the past to start running. If you begin small and build slowly, most healthy bodies will gradually learn to enjoy it.
Ana holds up a plain trainer and says that a comfortable shoe is enough. The research on very expensive shoes is mixed, so the best one is the one that fits.
That afternoon, Sam takes Joy to a sports shop, where a whole wall is covered in trainers. He feels lost, until a friendly assistant asks him a few simple questions.
Sam tries on several pairs and leaves a thumb's width of space in front of his toes. He walks and jogs a few steps up and down the shop, and the third pair feels right.
Blisters are the beginner's enemy, so Ana recommends soft socks that fit well. New shoes should be worn in gently, a little at a time, before any long run.
Some people love to run barefoot, but the science on this is not settled. Anyone who wants to try it should go very slowly on soft ground, and only for short spells.

Ana tells the group that different surfaces feel very different under the feet. Grass is softer, a pavement is firmer, and a mixture of both is probably kinder to the body than the same road every day.
Sam worries that he needs special clothes, but Ana says that he does not. A comfortable T-shirt and loose shorts are enough, and light layers keep him warm when it is cold.
Ana has asked everyone to walk briskly three times this week, so Sam does it in the evenings after work. At first he feels silly, but by the third walk he is looking forward to it.
Leila takes a marker pen and circles every Saturday on the family calendar. She says that the whole house is now part of the plan, and Joy promises to wake him up.
On Friday night, Sam lies awake, worried about his first real run. Leila reminds him that he has already done the hardest part, which was showing up.
On the second Saturday, Ana stands in front of the group and explains the plan. They will jog gently for one minute, then walk for two, and repeat this several times.
The group lines up on the path while Ana holds a silver whistle in the air. Sam's heart is already beating fast, and he has not even moved yet.
Sam starts the first jog too quickly and is soon red in the face. Ana jogs beside him and tells him to go slower than he thinks he needs to.
During the first walking break, Sam and Nadia compare notes in short, breathless sentences. They are both red in the face, but they agree that it was not as terrible as they feared.
They repeat the pattern again and again, jogging for one minute and walking for two. Frank hums an old song to keep time, and soon half the group is humming along.
Ana teaches the group something she calls the talk test. If you can say a few sentences while you run, your pace is about right, and if you cannot, you should slow down.
At the new pace, Sam is jogging so slowly that Frank could almost keep up at a fast walk. He feels a little embarrassed, but Ana tells him that this is exactly the right speed.
Sam wonders if there is a secret way to breathe while running. Ana says that there is not, and that he can breathe through his nose, his mouth or both.
Halfway through a jog, Sam feels a sharp pain in his side, which Ana calls a stitch. Scientists are not sure what causes it, but slowing down and breathing out slowly usually helps.
Ana shows the group a simple way to hold the body. Stand tall, let the shoulders drop, and look at the path ahead instead of at your feet.
Many beginners take steps that are too long, which makes each landing harder on the legs. Ana suggests short, quick steps, with the foot landing under the body.
Ana claps a steady rhythm and asks everyone to match their footsteps to it. The quick beat makes the steps shorter and lighter, and the whole group begins to patter along like rain.
Sam asks whether he should land on his heel or his toes. Ana says that runners do both, that the research is not clear, and that the foot should simply land under the body.
Ana tells the group to bend the elbows and swing the arms gently forward and back. She says the hands should be loose, as if holding a packet of crisps without crushing it.
Ana tells the group to check their faces, because a tight jaw can make the whole body tense. Sam unclenches his teeth, and he finds that his shoulders drop at the same time.
In the low morning sun, Sam sees his shadow stretching along the path ahead of him. It bobs up and down in a steady rhythm, and for the first time he thinks that he looks like a runner.
After the last jog, the group walks slowly to cool down while their breathing calms. Sam realises that about twenty minutes have passed, and that he did not once want to go home.
Ana hands out small notebooks and asks everyone to write one line after each run. She wants them to note how it felt, not how fast it was.
At home, Joy meets Sam at the door and asks whether he really ran. He says that he ran in little pieces, and she answers that the pieces still count.
That evening, Joy teaches Sam to run in the garden the way she does. She tells him to be light and bouncy, and to pretend that the grass is hot.
The next morning, Sam can hardly walk down the stairs because his legs are so sore. Ana says that mild soreness is normal, but that a sharp pain is a signal to stop.
Ana has told him that gentle movement often eases stiff muscles, so Sam walks once around the block. His legs complain at first, but after ten minutes they feel a little looser.
Sam lies on the sofa with his feet up, and Joy brings him water like a tiny nurse. Leila says that he looks like a man who has climbed a mountain.
Ana explains that a body does not become stronger during the run itself. It gets stronger afterwards, while it rests, so beginners should run on every other day.
On a rest day, Sam walks past his shoes ten times and longs to put them on. He remembers Ana's rule about stopping while you still want more, so he leaves them where they are.
At the office, Dev laughs at Sam's stiff walk and asks if he has been in a fight. When Sam says that he has started running, Dev goes quiet, and then says that he could never do it.
On Tuesday evening, Sam prepares for his first run on his own. He sets a timer on his phone to beep when it is time to jog and when it is time to walk.
Sam jogs slowly along his own street at dusk, trying to look as if he does this every day. His neighbour, Mr Okafor, waves from his gate, and his small dog, Biscuit, barks a cheer.
After the run, Sam writes a line in his notebook: “quiet, cold, proud.” Then he takes the green marker and ticks the day on the fridge calendar, which feels like a small victory.
Joy has been watching from the window, and she asks if she can come next time. Sam says yes at once, though he suspects that she will run circles around him.
In the second week, Joy asks if she can run with her father. She skips ahead, runs back, and turns every straight path into a game.
On Saturday, Ana welcomes Joy to the group with a high five. She tells everyone that children are the best teachers of running, because they have not yet learned to be afraid of it.
Joy runs beside her father without a sign of effort, and her face is calm and bright. Sam is a little jealous, but he is also so proud that his chest feels tight.
Joy shouts that she will race him to the next lamp post. Sam laughs, speeds up for a few seconds, and then slows down again, and he discovers that playing with speed is fun.
Now it is Sam's turn to invent a game, and he points to a big oak tree far ahead. They jog to it together, and they walk to the next one, and so on, all along the path.
