The science is not settled, she replied, and the feet and calves need a long time to adapt, so anyone curious should start on soft grass and for only a few minutes. For a beginner with a new pair of shoes and a full diary, she added with a smile, shoes were probably the simpler choice.

Different surfaces, Ana told the group, ask quite different things of the body, and the feet are the first to notice. Grass and packed earth are softer and more forgiving, while pavement is firmer and does exactly the same thing with every step. A varied route, she suggested, probably spreads the load more kindly than the same stretch of road day after day.

To Sam's relief, running turned out to need almost no special equipment, and Ana told him to wear whatever he found comfortable. An old T-shirt, a pair of loose shorts and a light jacket were all that most beginners needed, she said, and the fancy kit could wait. He laid the outfit out on the bed, and Joy gave it a solemn nod of approval.

Ana had set a simple task for the week, which was to walk briskly three times, and Sam took it more seriously than any assignment at work. On the first evening he felt self-conscious in his new shoes, but by the third he was striding along the river path as the sun went down. It occurred to him that he had spent years rushing between places without ever noticing how pleasant the journey could be.

On the fridge door, Leila circled the next twelve Saturdays in thick green marker pen, and declared that the entire household was now part of the plan. Joy volunteered to be the official alarm clock, a role she took with alarming enthusiasm. Sam looked at the circles and felt something he had not expected, which was the quiet, pleasant weight of being counted on.

On Friday night, Sam lay awake listening to the house settle, with a pair of new shoes beside the bed and a colony of butterflies in his stomach. Leila turned over, patted his arm and reminded him that the hardest part was already behind him, since he had walked through that park gate once and would do it again. Somewhere between the second and third attempt at sleep, he decided that she was right.

On the second Saturday, Ana explained that the whole group would begin with a pattern that many beginners use, called walk-run. They would jog gently for one minute, then walk for two, and repeat the cycle until about twenty minutes had passed. To Sam's surprise, the idea of the walking breaks felt less like failure than like a clever way of sharing the effort across the morning.

The group lined up along the path like runners at the start of a great race, though the finish line was only a lamp post a few hundred steps ahead. Ana raised a silver whistle to her lips and reminded them to start slower than they thought they should. Sam nodded wisely, and then ignored her advice completely, because his pride had other plans.

When the first whistle blew, Sam shot off along the path as if he were being chased, and within a minute his chest was heaving and his legs felt like wet sand. Ana jogged calmly alongside him and told him, with great gentleness, that his pace should feel almost embarrassingly slow. He tried again, and to his amazement he reached the end of the minute smiling instead of panting.

In the walking break, Sam found himself beside Nadia, who was scarlet in the face and smiling in spite of it. They compared sensations in short, breathless sentences, and discovered that both of them had been convinced that everyone else was finding it easy. It was a small revelation, and it did more for Sam's confidence than any amount of encouragement could have done.

The pattern repeated itself like a strange kind of music, one minute of effort followed by two of recovery, again and again around the park. Frank began to hum an old dance tune to keep the time, and before long half the group was humming with him, slightly out of tune. Sam realised, a little to his surprise, that he was smiling in the middle of a run.

Sam asked how fast a beginner ought to run, and Ana gave him a simple answer in the form of a game she called the talk test. You must be able to say a short sentence aloud without gasping, she explained, and that is all. If the words come out in broken pieces, she said, you are going too fast, and the cure is simply to slow down until a conversation becomes possible.

At the new pace, Sam was moving so slowly that a brisk walker could almost have kept up beside him, and his pride squirmed in protest. Ana, jogging alongside, assured him that this was precisely the right speed for a beginner, and that nobody in the history of running had ever got fitter by suffering on the first day. The slower he went, she promised, the further he would be able to go, and that, after all, was the point.

Sam had read that serious runners follow strict patterns of breathing, and he worried that he was doing it wrong. Ana reassured him that there was no magic method and that the best way to breathe is whichever feels natural, using the nose, the mouth, or both together. If his breath feels out of control, she added, the solution is almost always a slower pace.

Halfway through a jogging stretch, a sharp pain stabbed Sam in the side, and he clutched at his ribs in alarm. Ana told him that it was only a stitch, that scientists are still not certain what causes it, and that the usual cure is simply to slow down and breathe out steadily. Within a minute or two it had faded away, and he felt rather foolish for having been so worried.

Posture, Ana said, does not need to be perfect, but a few small habits make the run feel lighter. Imagine a string lifting you gently from the top of your head, let your shoulders drop away from your ears, and look at the path some distance ahead. Sam straightened up, and to his surprise his breathing felt a little easier at once.

Many beginners reach out with the front foot, as if they were trying to leap over a puddle, which makes each landing harder and slows the body down. Ana suggested shorter, quicker steps with the feet landing more nearly under the hips, although she was careful to say that the research on running form is not clear-cut. Sam tried it, and the whole stride began to feel lighter, like a quiet patter instead of a thump.

To help them feel a lighter stride, Ana clapped a steady, brisk rhythm and asked the group to land one foot on every beat. The quick pulse of the clapping shortened their steps without any effort, and the heavy thumping of a few minutes before gave way to a soft patter, like rain on a tin roof. Sam was amazed that something as simple as a clap could change the whole feeling of the run.

Sam had read heated arguments about whether to land on the heel, the middle or the front of the foot, and he asked Ana which was correct. Runners do all three, she replied, and the research has not shown that any one style suits everybody, so the best advice is to keep the steps short and the landing gentle. It was a relief to hear that there was no secret code to crack.

Tension, Ana explained, is a runner's silent thief, and it often hides in the fists and the shoulders. She told everyone to bend their elbows, swing their arms gently from front to back, and keep their hands as relaxed as if they were carrying a delicate egg. Sam looked down and found that he had been clenching his fists the whole morning.

Tension, Ana said, spreads through the body like water through a sponge, and one of its favourite hiding places is the jaw. She told the group to let their mouths fall slightly open and their faces go soft, even if they felt silly. Sam tried it, and discovered to his astonishment that his shoulders, his arms and even his legs seemed to loosen in sympathy.

The morning sun was low and golden, and it threw Sam's shadow far ahead of him along the path, where it bobbed and swung in a steady rhythm. He watched it for a while with growing amazement, because the figure on the grass looked entirely like a real runner. It was a small thing, but it gave him a quiet burst of confidence that lasted for the rest of the session.

After the final jog, the group walked slowly in a loose circle while their breathing settled and their faces turned from scarlet back to pink. Sam glanced at the park clock and realised that nearly twenty minutes had gone by, in which he had jogged seven times without falling apart once. It struck him that he had not felt so pleasantly worn out since he was a boy.

Before they left, Ana handed each beginner a cheap little notebook and asked them to write a single line after every run. She did not want times or distances, she explained, but a few honest words about how the run had felt, because those would reveal patterns that no stopwatch could. Sam wrote “slow, hard, surprisingly good,” and found that he was grinning at the page.

Joy was waiting at the front door with her arms folded and demanded to know whether her father had really run. Sam explained that he had run in seven little pieces, joined together with a good deal of walking, and he waited for her to laugh at him. She considered the matter with great seriousness and then announced that pieces counted, because a jigsaw is only a lot of pieces too.

That evening, in the back garden, Joy decided that her father needed lessons from an expert, and she appointed herself to the post. Run lightly, she instructed, as if the grass were hot, and let your arms be silly. Sam bounced obediently around the washing line, feeling ridiculous and delighted in equal measure, while Leila laughed at the kitchen window.

Sam woke the next day with legs so stiff that he descended the stairs backwards, one painful step at a time, to the delight of his daughter. Ana had warned him that this dull ache, which lasts a day or two, is common when muscles are doing something new. A sharp, sudden or lasting pain, she had added, is a different matter, and a good reason to stop and seek advice.

Ana had told him that gentle movement often eases stiff muscles better than lying still, so Sam went out on Sunday afternoon for a slow walk around the block. His legs grumbled bitterly for the first few hundred steps, like an old engine on a cold morning. After ten minutes the stiffness began to melt, and he returned home moving almost like a normal person.

By the afternoon Sam was installed on the sofa with his feet on a cushion, and Joy had appointed herself his nurse. She brought him water, a blanket he did not need and a stream of anxious questions about whether he could still feel his toes. Leila watched from the doorway with her arms folded, and said that he looked like a man who had just conquered a mountain.

It is a strange truth, Ana told the group, that you do not get fitter while you run but in the hours of recovery that follow. During the effort, you place a small stress on the body, and in the rest that follows the body rebuilds itself a little stronger than before. For that reason, beginners are wise to run only every second day, leaving the days in between for sleeping, walking and doing nothing at all.

On his rest day, Sam passed his running shoes in the hallway at least ten times, and each time they seemed to look at him reproachfully. Then he remembered Ana's third rule, which was to stop while you still feel you could do more, and he realised that this was exactly the position he was in. He made himself a cup of tea, sat down and took a deep, almost virtuous breath.

At the office on Monday, Sam's colleague Dev watched him lower himself into his chair like a man made of glass and asked whether he had been in a fight. When Sam confessed that he had started running, Dev's grin faded, and he said, in a quieter voice, that he had always wanted to but could never do it. Sam heard in that remark a very familiar echo of his own voice from a few weeks earlier.

On Tuesday evening, with nobody to blow a whistle for him, Sam turned to technology and set up an interval timer on his phone. It would beep once to tell him to jog for a minute and twice to tell him to walk for two, and he trusted it far more than he trusted his own willpower. He put the phone in his pocket, stepped out of the front door and felt oddly like a spy on a mission.

Running along his own street at dusk, Sam tried hard to look as if he did this every evening, though the curtains twitching in every window suggested that his neighbours knew better. Mr Okafor, who lived at number twelve, stood at his gate and raised a hand in solemn salute, while his small, round dog, Biscuit, barked what sounded like encouragement. Sam found, to his surprise, that being watched was not nearly as dreadful as he had feared.

Back in the kitchen, with his heart still tapping and his cheeks glowing, Sam wrote a line in the notebook that Ana had given him, which read “quiet, cold, proud.” Then he picked up the green marker from the fridge and put a firm tick beside Tuesday, as if he were marking a school exam he had at last managed to pass. Leila read the calendar over his shoulder, smiled at the new green tick and kissed him on the cheek.

Joy had watched his return from the upstairs window, and she appeared in the kitchen in her pyjamas and a pair of muddy trainers, asking whether she could run with him on Thursday. Sam, who had been dreading the day when his daughter would see him puffing along, found that he wanted nothing more. He said yes at once, though he suspected that she would run rings around him.

By the second week, Joy had grown so curious about her father's new habit that she begged to come along. She treated the run as one great game, skipping ahead, circling back, jumping over cracks and inventing rules that changed with every lamp post. Sam realised that she had never once looked at a watch, and that she seemed to enjoy herself far more than he did.

When Saturday came, Ana welcomed Joy to the group with a solemn high five and announced that she was the newest member of the coaching staff. Children, she told the beginners, are the best teachers of running, because nobody has yet convinced them that it is hard, boring or embarrassing. The adults looked at the girl bouncing on her toes and tried to remember what that felt like.

Joy ran beside her father without any sign of effort, humming, hopping over roots and chattering about a girl at school who had lost a tooth. Sam, meanwhile, was working with all his might, and he felt a sharp little prickle of envy that quickly melted into something warmer. It was one thing to watch your child grow, he thought, and quite another to watch her do something you had lost, and to realise that she was teaching you to find it again.

Joy pointed at a lamp post a hundred steps ahead and challenged her father to a race, and Sam, to his own surprise, accepted. He sped up for a few joyful seconds, collapsed into a gentle jog, and found that his legs had enjoyed the sudden change. Ana later told him that this kind of playful variation, mixing short quick bursts with easy running, has a name among coaches, but that it began as nothing more than a children's game.

Now it was Sam's turn to invent a game, and he pointed to a large oak tree a good way down the path. They would jog to the oak, he decided, then walk to the next tree, then jog again, and so on, until they reached the gate. Joy thought it was a brilliant idea, and she pretended that she had thought of it herself.

Joy's imagination was endless, and she invented a new game at nearly every bend in the path. They jogged like robots, waddled like ducks and floated like very slow cheetahs, and Sam laughed so hard that he forgot to look at his watch. It dawned on him that play was not the opposite of training but a perfectly good way of doing it.

After a fast stretch, Joy put a hand flat on her chest and asked, with enormous interest, why her heart went boom when she ran. Sam opened his mouth to answer, discovered that he knew only the vaguest things about it, and promised that they would find out together. The pleasure of not knowing, he realised, was that it gave them both something to look forward to.

Joy asked, with perfect politeness, why her father ran so slowly, since even the bus seemed faster. Sam explained that going slowly was the whole point, because a beginner who goes slowly can keep going for much longer than one who rushes. She weighed this carefully, and then appointed herself his official pace-keeper, with the right to shout at him whenever he sped up.

Frank and Joy discovered each other during the walking breaks, and it was a friendship that surprised everyone except the two of them. He taught her to produce a piercing whistle by stretching a blade of grass between her thumbs, and she taught him to skip, which he found much harder than driving a double-decker bus. Sam, walking a few steps behind, noticed that the retired bus driver was laughing louder than anyone in the park.

After every session, Ana produced an enormous flask of tea and a battered tin of biscuits, and the group collapsed on the grass in a contented circle. Nobody was in a hurry to leave, and the conversation rambled from knees to holidays to the proper way of making porridge. Sam sipped his tea and realised, with some surprise, that he now belonged to something, and that he had not expected to find it on a damp Saturday morning in a park.

Sam turned up for his third session carrying a bottle the size of a small bucket, which made Ana smile. For a short run, she said, a normal person who has had a normal day only needs to drink when thirsty, and forcing down large amounts can do more harm than good. Longer runs in the heat call for more care, but that was a problem for another year.

After the run, Sam asked whether the bright blue sports drinks in the shop window were something a runner needed. For short runs like theirs, Ana answered, plain water is perfectly good, and any normal drink at a normal meal will do the rest of the work. Her advice for the money he saved was to buy a decent pair of socks.

Sam wondered whether he needed protein shakes, energy gels or some secret diet, but Ana laughed at the idea. A beginner who runs for twenty or thirty minutes does well with ordinary meals made of simple, varied food, perhaps with a small snack such as a banana an hour beforehand. A heavy meal just before a run, she warned, is a good recipe for a stitch.

Experience taught Sam what no leaflet could, which was that a big lunch and a run do not make good companions. After a large meal he now waited a couple of hours before putting on his shoes, and before an early run he settled for something light, such as a slice of toast. The exact timing differed from person to person, Ana said, so the secret was to experiment calmly and note what worked in his notebook.

When the conversation drifted towards diets and calories, Ana raised her hand like a traffic officer. In her group, she declared, running was never to be treated as a punishment for eating, and nobody would be asked to step on the scales. Joy, listening to this with a biscuit in each hand, thought it was the most sensible rule she had ever heard.

Nadia sat beside Ana on the bench, twisting a corner of her jacket, and admitted that she was afraid of being judged by everyone she met on the path. Ana told her gently that nobody in the group was measuring bodies, and that what the beginners shared was far more interesting than their shapes. It was a small conversation, but Sam noticed that Nadia ran differently afterwards, with her head a little higher.

Since the running began, Sam's appetite had returned with a vengeance, and Leila rose to the occasion with big, simple family dinners of rice, beans and plenty of vegetables. Joy observed that her father now ate like a horse, which Sam took as a compliment, since horses, as everyone knows, are excellent runners. There was no need for anything exotic, Ana had said, only ordinary, varied food and a little attention to what made him feel good.

On Friday morning, Dev appeared at Sam's desk with a box of doughnuts and a look of mischievous challenge. Sam hesitated for exactly one second, then took the biggest one and ate it with open delight, since Ana's group had taught him that a treat is part of a happy life and not a crime. Dev laughed, and then, to Sam's amusement, asked a little shyly how the running was going.

Joy declared that her father's water bottle was far too plain for a serious runner, and she spent a whole Sunday afternoon covering it with stickers, stars and a large green rocket. Sam inspected the result with the gravity of an art critic and announced that it was now his lucky bottle. It went with him on every run after that, and it never failed to make other runners smile.

By the third week, Sam felt stronger than he had in a decade, and a dangerous idea began to take root in his head. Ana's careful plan, he decided, was designed for the timid, and surely a man of his new fitness could do a good deal more. It did not occur to him that this was the very thought Ana's first rule had been written to prevent.

On Monday, Sam added an extra run to the week, and on Wednesday he added another, ignoring the rest day that stood between them in the plan. He also ran faster than he had been told to, partly because it felt wonderful and partly because he wanted to prove that he could. His body, which had been trying politely to send him a message, was being outvoted by his enthusiasm.

For three days in a row he ran, each time a little longer and a little faster than before, and each evening he felt like a champion. In his notebook he wrote the single word unstoppable, underlined it twice, and went to bed with a warm sense of invincibility. Unfortunately, his left knee had also been keeping a note, and it was about to read it aloud.

In the third week, a sharp pain stabbed at the side of Sam's knee halfway through the run, and he stopped on the spot, cross with himself. Ana told him he had done exactly the right thing, because running through real pain can turn a small problem into a long one. She told him to rest for a few days, and to see a doctor or a physiotherapist if it did not settle.

Afterwards, Ana crouched beside him on the bench and asked exactly what he had done during the week. Sam confessed, with a guilty look, about the extra runs, and she nodded slowly without any sign of surprise. She reminded him that she was a coach and not a doctor, and that anything that did not settle was a matter for a professional.

Sam spent the evening sunk in gloom, convinced that his whole twelve-week adventure had been wrecked by his own stupidity. Joy, who had been watching him with her chin on her hand, vanished upstairs and returned with a get-well card on which she had drawn an enormous knee with a smile and two eyes. Sam laughed out loud for the first time all day, and the gloom lifted, if only a little.

Dr Rao examined the knee with calm, practised fingers, bending it, pressing it and asking him to walk across the room. She found nothing alarming, and told him that in his case a few days of rest and a gradual return to running should be enough. She added that every knee is different, and that he should come back at once if the pain returned or got worse.

During his week of rest, Sam learned that a runner is not only a pair of legs, but a body that needs strength throughout. Ana showed him squats, calf raises and a plank, to be done twice a week at home, and said that research suggests strength work may help reduce running injuries. Joy copied every movement with great seriousness, and she was a much better plank than her father.

When Sam wondered aloud whether he had ruined everything, Ana laughed and told him about the winter she had sprained her own ankle by training too hard for a race. She had spent six weeks on the sofa, she said, feeling like the most foolish coach in the county, and she had returned stronger and wiser than before. Setbacks happen to everyone who runs, she said, and the clever ones simply learn from them.

Looking at Sam's knee, Ana said that the most common story among runners is a happy beginning that ends in an injury, because enthusiasm grows faster than the body's strength. Doing too much too soon is widely seen as one of the main causes. Coaches often quote a rule of adding no more than ten percent a week, but Ana called it a rough guide that has not been proved, and said that listening to the body matters more.

After a week of rest, Sam returned to the path, and Ana had him step back to an earlier stage of the plan, with shorter jogs and longer walks. He tested every stride as carefully as a man crossing ice, but the knee stayed quiet, and by the end of the session it had stopped even being mentioned. He promised himself that he would never be so greedy again, though he suspected that the promise would be tested.

Calf raises were the simplest exercise of all, Ana told him: rise slowly onto the toes, hold for a moment, and lower again. Sam did them at the kitchen sink while the kettle boiled, with one hand resting on the counter and an expression of grim concentration. By the end of the week he could feel the muscles at the back of his legs, which had been asleep for twenty years, beginning to wake up.

The plank looked easy until Sam tried it, resting on his forearms and toes with his body in a single straight line, like a plank in a builder's yard. Ana had said that the exercise worked the stomach, the back and the hips together, the very muscles that keep a runner upright when the legs begin to tire. Joy counted the seconds aloud with the ruthless precision of a stopwatch, and she was delighted to discover how quickly her father started to tremble.

Running, Ana pointed out, is really a long series of small leaps from one leg to the other, so it pays to train the muscles that keep the ankle and the hip steady. She suggested standing on one leg for half a minute at a time, for instance while brushing the teeth. Sam wobbled like a tree in a gale at first, and spat toothpaste on the mirror, but the improvement was swift enough to encourage him.

Lying on his back with his knees bent and his feet flat, Sam pushed his hips towards the ceiling and held them there for a slow count of three. This simple movement, known as a bridge, wakes up the large muscles of the buttocks and the backs of the legs, which Ana had already described as a runner's engine room. After ten repetitions he lay on the carpet looking at the light fitting, feeling oddly accomplished.

Within a fortnight the whole family had joined in, and Sunday evenings in the living room began to resemble a small and very cheerful gymnasium. Leila performed her squats with a serious face, Sam grunted over his planks, and Joy counted aloud and awarded marks for style. It was the first time in years, Sam realised, that the walls of his home had heard so much laughter at once.

Strong muscles and tendons, Ana explained, can share the load of each running step, so that the joints are not left to absorb all of it alone. Research suggests that regular strength work may lower the risk of injury, although no exercise can promise that a runner will never be hurt. She said it twice, to be sure that everybody heard the second half of the sentence.

On his rest days, Sam took gentle evening walks beside the river with Leila, and he noticed a number of things that had escaped him on his hurried runs. A heron stood like a grey statue in the shallows, the willows trailed their fingers in the water, and the whole town smelled faintly of rain. He began to understand that rest was not a gap in the plan but a part of it.

Before each session, Ana led the group through a short warm-up of brisk walking, gentle leg swings and a few easy knee lifts, so that the muscles were awake before the work began. Sam asked whether he should also stretch for a long time, and she answered that the evidence on stretching before exercise is mixed, and so she kept it brief. What mattered most, she said, was that you began slowly and let the body warm itself up.

At the end of each session, Ana never allowed the group to stop dead, but sent them on a few minutes of slow walking while their hearts and breathing settled. Stretching afterwards, she said, was perfectly fine for anyone who enjoyed it, although the research on its benefits is mixed and nobody should force a painful stretch. Sam stretched his calves against a tree, looked at the sky and felt thoroughly content.

At the end of the fourth week, Sam drew a firm green tick beside another circled Saturday and stood back to look at the fridge. A month ago he could not have run for a minute without gasping, and now he had a calendar full of ticks to prove that something had changed. He did not yet know that the next few weeks would bring his first real taste of joy.

Since he began running, Sam had noticed that he fell asleep faster and woke feeling more refreshed, although he was careful not to claim that this was scientific proof. Ana said that sleep is the time when the body repairs the small tears and strains of the day, and that people who skimp on it often feel tired during their runs. When your legs feel heavy, she told him, the right answer is often an earlier bedtime and not an extra mile.

After a restless night with a noisy neighbour and a worrying email, Sam woke feeling heavy, dull and rather sorry for himself. Remembering Ana's advice, he skipped that evening's run, ate an early supper and was asleep before nine o'clock. The next morning he woke clear-headed and light-footed, and the lost run seemed an excellent investment.

Ana was careful to say that she was no sleep expert, but she passed on a few habits that had helped many of her runners. Go to bed at about the same hour each night, she suggested, keep the bedroom dark and quiet, and leave the phone in another room. Sam, who usually fell asleep with a screen glowing on his chest, gave the idea a nervous but open-minded trial.

The heart, Ana reminded the group, is a muscle like any other, and it grows stronger when it is asked to work regularly and gently. After weeks of steady training, it can push more blood around the body with each beat, which is why the resting heart rate of many regular runners becomes slower. Sam put two fingers on his wrist that evening and, to his delight, felt a calm, steady rhythm.

That evening Sam showed Joy how to find the pulse at the wrist with two fingers, and they sat side by side on the sofa counting the beats against the clock. Hers was faster than his, which puzzled them both until Ana explained, a few days later, that a child's heart normally beats faster than a grown-up's. Joy took this as proof that she was the more athletic of the two, and Sam did not argue.

A pounding heart and heavy breathing, Ana told the group, are normal parts of effort, and they ease again when you slow down. Chest pain, dizziness, a feeling that you might faint or a heartbeat that seems wrong, however, are signals to stop at once and seek medical help. She said it gravely and without drama, and it was the one occasion on which not even Frank made a joke.

A neighbour had warned Sam that running would wreck his knees, and the worry had followed him around for weeks. Ana explained that bones respond to gentle pressure by becoming denser, and that studies of recreational runners have generally not found more knee arthritis than in people who do not run. Still, she said, individual bodies differ, and anyone with a joint problem should ask their doctor.

People often imagine that running enlarges the lungs, Ana said, but the lungs themselves change very little. What improves, as far as scientists can tell, is the way the heart delivers blood and the way the muscles take oxygen from it, so that the same effort starts to feel gentler. Sam thought of the first twenty steps in the park and marvelled at how much had changed without any sign of it on the outside.

One morning that week, Sam reached the top of three flights of office stairs and realised that he was not gasping at all. He stood on the landing, checking his breathing like a doctor, and found it calm and even. It was such a small thing, and yet it felt like the clearest proof so far that his body was changing.

Dev had been watching his colleague with growing curiosity, and one lunchtime he finally asked what exactly had happened to him. Sam told him the whole story, from the twenty steps in the park to the walk-run plan, and ended by saying that it had all begun with a single minute. Dev did not promise anything, but he asked for the address of the park, and Sam took that as a very good sign.

Halfway through his fifth week, Sam suddenly felt something like a warm glow spreading through his chest, a lightness that made the hill seem to flatten beneath him. Some runners call this a runner's high and have long linked it to chemicals in the brain, but researchers are still arguing about which chemicals matter and why. Not everyone experiences it, Ana said, and it is a pleasant bonus instead of a goal.

Joy wanted to know whether a runner's high meant that you left the ground, and she tested the theory by jumping as high as she could. Sam explained that it was a warm, happy feeling that arrived without warning, like a present left on the doorstep. He added honestly that it did not come every time, and that it would be silly to run in order to chase it.

For many years, the popular explanation was that the brain releases chemicals called endorphins during exercise and that these produce the happy glow. More recent studies suggest that other chemicals may be involved as well, and the truth is probably more tangled than a single neat answer. Ana encouraged the group to enjoy the feeling when it came, and not to worry about the puzzle.

Several members of the group said that running cleared their heads and softened the sharp edges of a stressful week, and Sam had begun to feel the same. Ana was quick to add that running is not a treatment for any illness, and that anyone whose low mood or worry lasts for weeks should talk to a doctor and not simply lace up their shoes. A good habit can support a person, she said, but it cannot replace proper care.

On the sixth Saturday, the sky was grey, rain was tapping at the window, and every sensible part of Sam wanted to stay in bed. Ana had warned him that motivation comes and goes, so she had taught him a trick of making the task so small that it is impossible to refuse, which meant putting on his shoes and going out for ten minutes. Twenty minutes later he was still plodding happily along the path, soaked to the skin, grinning like a fool, and quietly delighted that he had not given in.

To Sam's surprise, nearly everyone else had turned up as well, standing in the park in a rainbow of waterproofs with water dripping from their noses. Nadia had a bin bag over her shoulders, Frank wore a hat that belonged on a fishing boat, and Joy was splashing in every puddle she could find. They agreed, once the first few minutes had passed, that the hardest part of the whole exercise had been leaving the house.

Habits, Ana said, are not built by willpower but by making the right thing easy and the wrong thing a little harder. Sam kept his shoes beside the front door, laid out his kit the night before and ran on the same days each week, so that he never had to decide whether to go. After a month, it felt less like a choice than like brushing his teeth.

A crisis at work kept Sam in the office until nine one evening, and he missed his run and felt a small sting of guilt. When he confessed to Ana on Saturday, she looked at him as though he had told her that it had rained on Tuesday. One missed run is nothing, she said, and the only run that matters is the next one.

When Nadia missed two Saturdays in a row, Sam began to worry that she had given up, and he knew from his own experience how easily that could happen. He sent her a short, honest message to say that the group missed her, that he had been just as scared as she was at the beginning, and that he would wait for her at the gate. Then he put the phone down and spent the rest of the evening hoping, with his fingers crossed.

On Saturday, to Sam's enormous relief, Nadia was standing at the gate in a pair of spotless shoes, and the whole group burst into applause. She blushed to the roots of her hair and admitted that it had been his message that made her put the shoes on. They jogged the first minute side by side, and Sam realised that he was no longer the new one but someone who could help.

Weather is no reason to stop, Ana told the group, but it does call for a little thought. On cold days, a few thin layers are better than one thick coat, because you can take one off as you warm up, while in summer it is wise to run in the shade and slow down. When the light is poor, she added, bright or reflective clothes help drivers to notice you from a safe distance.

A spell of hot weather arrived, and Ana moved the Saturday session to the cool of the evening. She told everyone to run more slowly than usual, to wear a hat and to take water with them, and she watched the group closely for any sign of trouble. Nobody complained, and the pink light over the park was a reward in itself.

On a bitterly cold morning, with frost glittering on the grass, Ana told the group to wear hats and gloves and to give themselves a longer warm-up than usual. The first few minutes are the hardest, she said, and after that the body begins to generate its own heat. Sam, who had imagined that he would hate running in the cold, was surprised to find the crisp air strangely delicious.

When the evenings began to darken, Sam went back to the sports shop and bought a bright yellow vest with silver reflective strips. Wearing it made him feel rather like a road worker, but a driver could now see him from a long way off, which was a considerable comfort. Joy, who thought it was the finest garment her father had ever owned, asked to borrow it for her teddy bear.

Safety, Ana said, is the dullest part of running and the one that matters most. Tell somebody where you are going and when you will be back, carry a phone, run on a pavement where you can, and keep the volume of your headphones low enough to hear a car or a bicycle bell. If there is no pavement, she added, run facing the oncoming traffic so that you can see what is coming.

Following Ana's advice, Sam wrote his name, his address and Leila's phone number on a card, and tucked it into the pocket of his shorts. Before every solo run he also told Leila which way he was going and when he expected to be back, a habit that she appreciated more than he had expected. It was a dull little ritual, but it let both of them relax and enjoy the evening without worrying.

Curious about all the music he had heard others running to, Sam tried a pair of headphones on a quiet evening and enjoyed the beat in his ears. Then a bicycle bell rang right behind him, and he leapt sideways like a startled cat, and was forced to admit that he had not heard it coming. After that he kept the volume low, or used only one earphone, so that the world could still get a word in.

One evening Biscuit escaped from his lead and set off after Sam along the pavement with a volley of delighted barking, and Sam's first instinct was to sprint. He remembered, just in time, that running away tends to turn a dog's curiosity into a game, so he slowed to a walk, kept calm and spoke to the dog in a low voice. Biscuit lost interest and sat down, and Mr Okafor, arriving breathless, apologised twenty times.

As the dark evenings drew in, Sam stuck to well-lit streets and busy paths, and he avoided the quiet corners of the park once the sun had set. Whenever possible he invited someone from the group to come along, because company is both safer and more entertaining than the best of music. It was a small adjustment to his routine, and it cost him nothing at all.

Joy pointed out, on a bright morning, that her father's nose had turned the colour of a boiled prawn, and Sam had to admit that she had a point. The sun can burn even on cool days, Ana had warned, so he learned to wear a cap and to put sun cream on his face, arms and legs before every run. It was another tiny habit, and he added it to the list with a sigh and a smile.

Sam found that the Saturday group was made up of an unlikely mix of ages, shapes and speeds, from students to grandparents. One of them, Maria, was sixty-eight years old and had been running for thirty years, and she jogged beside Sam and chatted all the way round the park. Having someone to meet, she said, makes it much easier to turn up on days when the sofa is calling.

Maria told Sam that she had started running at thirty-eight, in the rare quiet hour after her children were in bed, because she wanted something that belonged only to her. She had been slow and clumsy at the start, she said, and she was still not fast, but she had not missed a season in thirty years. Sam found that last fact more impressive than any trophy he had ever seen in a cabinet.

Maria explained that, in her experience, a body takes a little longer to recover as the years pass, so she allowed herself more rest between runs than she had in her thirties. She also did her strength exercises with the faithfulness of a person brushing her teeth, which she believed was the real reason she had stayed injury-free. Age, she said, is not a reason to stop, only a reason to be a little wiser.

Maria invited Sam to the easy Tuesday evening run of her running club, which welcomed every speed from a determined shuffle to a gentle gallop. The people who gathered under the lamp post were a cheerful mixture of students, nurses, grandparents and a postman who talked from the first step to the last. Sam shook a dozen hands and felt, for the second time that year, that he had walked into the right place.

With Maria beside him, Sam found that the minutes disappeared like coins into a fountain, because talking made the effort seem lighter and the park shorter. They discussed his job, her grandchildren, the best way to cook lentils and the question of whether cats are secretly cleverer than dogs. When they finally stopped, he realised that he had been running for a quarter of an hour without once checking his watch.

Maria cheerfully admitted that she had never won a race in her life and did not expect to start now. What she had won, she said, was thirty years of mornings that began better than they would have otherwise, and a circle of friends she would never have met on a sofa. She put the matter in a single sentence, which Sam wrote in his notebook: you are always glad you went.

The club's route led through an old wood on the edge of town, along a narrow path that Sam had never known existed. Sunlight fell through the leaves in golden coins, and the only sounds were their footsteps, their steady breathing and a distant woodpecker. It astonished him that such a place had been waiting so close to his front door all those years, patient and unnoticed.

At the far side of Elm Park there was a steady hill, and Sam eyed it as if it were a mountain. Ana told him that nobody expects a beginner to run up it, so he should shorten his steps, lean forward slightly and walk the steepest part with no shame whatever. Going downhill, she added, calls for care, since the legs absorb more force, and a controlled, relaxed stride is better than a rush.

At the top of the hill, Maria showed Sam how she ran down it, which was with great care and a slightly comical air of calm. Her steps were short and quick, her knees a little bent, her arms loose and her eyes fixed on the path a few strides ahead. She did not fight the slope, she said, and she did not let it carry her away either.

On Sunday afternoon, Sam and Joy climbed the big hill together, walking the steep parts and jogging the rest, and they arrived at the top pink-faced and triumphant. From there the whole town lay spread out below them like a model, with the roofs, the river and the tiny moving cars all looking small and friendly. Joy pointed out their own house and the lamp post where she planned to beat him next time.

In the eighth week, Ana gathered the group on the grass and announced that they would try something new, which was to jog for twenty minutes without a single walking break. The pace would be so gentle, she promised, that they would be able to chat all the way round, and anyone who needed a break could take one with her blessing. Sam's stomach performed a small somersault, because twenty minutes sounded like a very long time.

Sam was so nervous before the test that his hands were damp, and Ana noticed at once. She reminded him of the talk test, told him to start more slowly than he thought he should, and advised him to treat the whole experiment as a long, gentle conversation with his own legs. It was the kind of advice that sounded like nothing and turned out to be everything.

The first five minutes were far easier than Sam had feared, and the group settled into a comfortable rhythm, chatting about holidays and the price of bread as though they were strolling to the shops. Sam kept checking his breath against the talk test, and each time it passed with room to spare. He began to wonder whether the whole thing was a trick, and whether the real test was still to come.

Somewhere in the middle, the cheerful rhythm began to fray, and Sam's legs felt as though somebody had quietly filled his shoes with sand. He talked to himself in the kindest voice he could manage, the way he would talk to Joy, and broke the remaining time into tiny pieces, only as far as the next tree, then the next. The trick worked far better than he expected, and the middle slowly slid behind him.

With five minutes to go, Sam spotted two familiar figures beside the path ahead, one tall and one small, with a flask of tea held aloft like a torch. He counted his breaths in fours, kept his pace steady and resisted a powerful temptation to sprint, because he had learned the hard way that enthusiasm in the final stretch is the cheapest way to hurt a knee. The two figures grew slowly larger, and his chest grew tighter for reasons that had nothing to do with effort.

In the eighth week, Sam looked at his watch, saw that twenty minutes had passed, and realised with a jolt that he had not walked once. Eight weeks earlier, he had been wheezing after twenty steps, and now he was jogging along contentedly with the sun on his back. When he finally stopped, he wiped his eyes and told Ana that it must be the wind.

Leila and Joy rushed to hug him, the group burst into applause, and Ana poured a cup of tea with a flourish. Sam confessed that two months earlier he could not have believed this was possible, and that even a week ago he had half expected to fail. Ana replied that she had believed it all along, and that this was the whole secret of her job.

In the ninth week, Sam had a terrible run, in which his legs felt like lead, every hill looked like a wall, and he wondered whether his earlier progress had been an illusion. Ana was entirely unworried and told him that improvement is never a straight line, that a bad day is usually caused by poor sleep, stress or tired muscles, and that even Olympic runners suffer from them. Two days later, after a good night's sleep and a day of complete rest, he ran as lightly as a deer and wondered what had worried him.

Ana explained that the surprising secret of many successful runners is that they run slowly most of the time, which leaves their legs fresh for the occasional harder effort. For the group, she suggested that most sessions should be easy and conversational, with perhaps one livelier session each week in which they pick up the pace for short stretches. The rest of the secret, she said with a smile, was simply patience, which no shop in the world is able to sell.

On one session each week, Ana let the group pick up the pace for a few short stretches, which she described as comfortably hard. You should still be able to say a few words, she explained, but not whole sentences, and each fast stretch should end while you still feel in control. It was never a race, she repeated, and the person who finished the day with a smile had run the session best.

Sam found that a rest day did not have to mean doing nothing, and on one of them he took Joy swimming at the local pool. Ana encouraged this kind of variety, which coaches call cross-training, because swimming, cycling and brisk walking can build fitness while giving the running muscles a break. It also, she said, protects you from becoming bored, which is a quiet danger for anyone who wants to keep a habit for years.

On another rest day, Sam and Joy took their bicycles out along a quiet lane lined with hedges and blackberries. Pedalling worked his legs in a different way from running, and left the tired muscles with a feeling of gentle use rather than strain. Joy, who rode a good thirty metres ahead and rang her bell at every bend, declared it the best kind of rest there was.

On Sunday morning, Sam and Leila went for a long country walk up the hill behind the town, with a flask of tea and a bag of apples. Walking, he reflected, was exercise too, and perhaps the best kind, because it asked nothing of him except to put one foot in front of the other and look around. It felt good to spend a rest day with the person who had circled all those Saturdays.

Many runners, Ana explained, build an easier week into their plans every few weeks, so that the body has time to absorb the work it has done. There is no single correct schedule, she said, and the evidence for any particular pattern is limited, but the principle of an occasional lighter week is widely trusted. Sam, who had once believed that more was always better, wrote the idea in his notebook with a thick line under it.

On Tuesday, running at the club's easy pace, Sam kept going for twenty-five minutes, the longest he had run since he was a boy. When he glanced at his watch at the end and understood what he had done, he let out a shout of pure delight that startled a pigeon off the nearest wall. Maria, running beside him, simply nodded as if she had known it all along.

Joy challenged her father to run all the way around the park, and she shot away at such speed that she looked like a rocket. Within three minutes she was bent over beside a bench, gasping, as Sam passed her at his slow and steady pace, and she could not help laughing at herself. The lesson, he told her kindly, is that the beginning of a long run should always feel too easy.

Even pacing, Ana told the group, is the quiet secret of every long run, and the commonest mistake is to start too quickly because the legs feel fresh. The first kilometre should feel almost too easy, she said, since the energy you save at the beginning is exactly the energy you will need at the end. Sam recalled Joy bent over beside the bench and understood the lesson in his bones.

Sam put the lesson into practice on a loop of Elm Park that took him about six minutes to jog, and he ran it three times, trying to make each lap exactly like the one before. The first lap felt almost embarrassingly gentle, the second felt comfortable, and the third felt strong, which was precisely the pattern that Ana had described. He sat on a bench afterwards with the quiet satisfaction of a man who has solved a small puzzle.

Ana pinned up a map of the fun run course, a winding ribbon of red ink that passed through two parks, along the riverbank and under the old stone bridge. Five kilometres, she told them, is a little over three miles, and nobody would think any less of a runner who walked some of it. Sam traced the route with his finger and found that his heart was thumping with excitement rather than dread.

At the end of the session, Ana handed out the entry forms for the fun run, and a hush fell over the circle. Sam read the page twice, wrote his name in careful capital letters with a hand that shook only a little, and gave it back before his courage could slip away. It was no longer a plan, he realised, but a promise, and he found that he liked the weight of it.

Joy announced that she would be the official supporter at the finish line, and she began work on a banner at once, using an old bedsheet and every pot of paint in the house. The words Go Dad stretched across it in enormous letters of several colours, followed by a smaller and rather messy sun. Leila, surveying the damage to the kitchen table, said that it was the finest banner she had ever seen, and she meant it.

Ana wrote the plan for the last four weeks on her whiteboard, and the beginners copied it into their notebooks with a certain reverence. The runs would grow a little longer, the easy days would stay easy, and the final week, which caused a gasp, would be lighter than all the others. She reminded them that the plan was a map and not a law, and that they could adjust it whenever their bodies asked.

In the tenth week, Sam ran for thirty minutes without stopping, further than he had gone since he was a boy, and he did it at an easy, conversational pace. When the time was up he realised that he could have gone on a little longer, which was exactly the feeling Ana had said to look for. For the first time, the five kilometres of the fun run seemed like a real and reachable place.

Sam finally admitted to Ana that his greatest fear was finishing last and being laughed at by a crowd of strangers. Someone always finishes last, she said, and in her experience the people at the back were often the bravest, because they were out there longest, and the crowd always saved its loudest cheer for them. Besides, she added with a grin, she had been last in plenty of races herself, and she had never once been laughed at.

Nadia and Frank had entered as well, and they held up their entry forms in the park like winners of a lottery. The three of them agreed to start together near the back, to keep an easy pace and to meet at the finish for tea, whatever the clock said. Sam felt a warm rush of gratitude for the odd little band of strangers who had somehow become his friends.

Over a cup of tea, Maria shared a few of the lessons that thirty years of races had taught her. Start near the back, she said, keep the pace gentle in the first kilometre, thank the volunteers who hand out the water, and remember to look up from your feet now and then. A race, in her view, was a street party in which everybody happened to be wearing running shoes.

On Thursday, Sam collected his race number from a table in the town hall and read the leaflet with the thoroughness of a man studying a legal contract. It told him where to park, where the toilets were, where the water stations stood and what time the start was, and he checked every detail twice. Joy, standing on tiptoe to read over his arm, announced that she would find the finish line herself.

Ana advised everyone to treat their last long run as a dress rehearsal, wearing the exact clothes and shoes they planned to use on the day and eating the same breakfast beforehand. Sam did as he was told and found that the shirt rubbed slightly under one arm, which was precisely the sort of discovery the rehearsal was designed to make. He changed to an older shirt and was pleased with the lesson, if not with the sore patch.

Ana showed the group a few simple tricks to prevent rubbing and blisters on the big day. A dab of petroleum jelly where the skin tends to chafe, a plaster over a tender spot and a pair of dry, well-fitting socks, she said, are usually all that a beginner needs. Sam rubbed some jelly on the sore patch under his arm and sniffed it suspiciously, like a chemist at work.

Late one evening, Sam confessed to Leila that he was worried he was not ready, and that the whole enterprise might be a foolish dream. She counted on her fingers everything he had done in ten weeks, from the first wobbling minute in the park to the thirty-minute run, by way of the knee and the doctor and the bad days. By the time she reached the end of her list she had run out of fingers and he had run out of arguments.

The week before the fun run, Ana made an announcement that astonished the beginners, which was that they should now run less. This practice, known as tapering, gives the muscles time to recover fully from weeks of training, so that the legs feel fresh and eager on the day itself. Sam obeyed, though he found it harder to rest than to run, and he spent the week watching the calendar.

During the easy week, Sam felt as restless as a caged tiger, and every small twinge in his body seemed to announce a catastrophe. He imagined a sore throat, a stiff ankle and a mysterious pain behind his ear, until Ana assured him that nervous runners all over the world were suffering the same phantom symptoms. If something truly hurt, she said, he should say so, but most of these aches would vanish with the starting whistle.

In the last few days before the run, Sam rested, drank water when he was thirsty and ate his usual meals, which meant a great deal of rice and beans. He went to bed early, politely refused a mysterious curry that Dev tried to tempt him with at work and felt strangely calm. All the work, he reflected, was already in the bank, and there was nothing left to do but wait.

On Thursday, Sam took one short, easy run of about ten minutes, just enough to remind his legs of what they were for. They felt springy, fresh and eager, like a dog that has been shut indoors on a sunny day, and he had to remind himself repeatedly not to speed up. He walked home grinning, with the oddest sensation that his body was ready to burst out of his skin.

On Friday evening, Sam laid out his clothes on the bed like a soldier preparing for inspection, and Joy took charge of the number. She attached it to the front of his shirt with four safety pins, one at each corner, and checked every one of them three times with her tongue between her teeth. When she had finished, she patted the paper flat and declared that it would not come off in a hurricane.

On the night before the fun run, the family ate a simple, familiar dinner of pasta and vegetables, and nobody mentioned the next day except Joy. The conversation drifted to school, to Biscuit's latest escape and to the question of whether goldfish dream, and Sam felt his nerves unwind with every minute. By nine o'clock he was in bed, and by half past, to his own astonishment, he was asleep.

On the morning of the fun run, Sam woke before the alarm with a stomach full of butterflies and a number to pin on his shirt. Ana had given him one golden rule, which was to try nothing new on race day, so he put on his usual shoes, ate his usual porridge and drank his usual tea. It all felt oddly ordinary for such a big day, and that, he realised as he laced his shoes, was exactly the whole point.

The family walked into town through streets that had been transformed overnight, with balloons tied to the lamp posts, a brass band warming up on the corner and hundreds of runners streaming towards the park. A man dressed as a giant carrot was doing stretches beside the fountain, and Joy begged to be photographed with him, which Leila did while Sam's stomach rolled over once more. It was impossible, he thought, to feel entirely terrified in the middle of a street party.

Near the start, Ana gathered her beginners in a tight circle, all in their bright shirts and with their numbers pinned to their chests. She reminded them one last time to start slower than they felt like starting, to walk whenever their bodies asked and, above all, to enjoy it, since nobody was paying them to be miserable. Then she looked at each of them in turn and said that she was prouder than she knew how to say.

At the start line, hundreds of people shuffled and stretched together, including teenagers in bright shorts, grandparents in woolly hats and a man dressed as a banana. Sam had feared that he would be the slowest person there, but a glance around the crowd made him realise that everyone was running their own private race against their own private worries. Joy squeezed his hand tightly, he squeezed it back, and a moment later the whistle blew and the whole crowd surged gently forward.

The first minute was chaos, as a flood of runners surged past Sam on both sides, and his pride whispered that he ought to follow them. He remembered Joy beside the bench, Ana's circle and every lesson on pacing, and he let the fast ones go with a smile. Within five minutes the road had opened out, and he found himself running among people who were just as slow as he was and just as happy.

The streets were lined with spectators who clapped, rang cowbells and shouted encouragement at every runner, whether fast or slow, while a brass band thumped out a march on the corner. Complete strangers called out to Sam as though they had known him all their lives, and he was astonished by how much their voices seemed to lift his legs. He waved back like a politician, and a small child with a balloon waved at him.

Frank, who had been jogging beside Sam since the first corner, suddenly found a hidden reserve of energy and trotted ahead with a cheerful wave. He called over his shoulder that he would see him at the finish, and he sounded as astonished as anybody by his own announcement. Sam laughed aloud, held to his easy pace and trusted that the old bus driver would not run out of steam before the end.

The first half of the course was a delight, winding through two parks, along the bright riverbank and under the old stone bridge near the spot where Sam had so often walked with Leila. The sun glittered on the water, the pace felt almost lazy, and for several minutes he forgot altogether that he was running a race. It was only when he passed the first water station that the reality returned, and it returned with a smile.

Around the three-kilometre mark, the cheerful chatter of the start was replaced by the sound of laboured breathing, and Sam's legs began to scream for a rest. He did what Ana had taught him, counting his steps in fours, relaxing his shoulders and thinking only of the next lamp post rather than the distance still to go. Somewhere ahead, past the bend and the last of the trees, he knew that Joy would be waiting for him.

Nadia, who had been struggling behind, caught up with Sam at the four-kilometre mark, and they ran together for a while without saying much. Each of them was too busy breathing to talk, but each was quietly glad of the other's company, and the silence between them was warm and easy. When one slowed down, the other slowed down too, and neither mentioned it afterwards.

With one kilometre to go, Sam saw a familiar figure at the roadside, waving a piece of cardboard above his head. It was Dev, who had told nobody he was coming, and the sign said, in large and wobbly capitals, “Next year, me.” Sam laughed so hard that he nearly lost his rhythm, and he blew a kiss across the heads of the crowd.

In the last two hundred metres, Joy jumped over the barrier, took her father's hand and dragged him towards the finish line, shouting that he must run faster. They crossed it together, with their arms in the air and their faces wet with sweat and laughter, and a volunteer hung a medal around Sam's neck. His time, he later discovered, was nothing to boast about, but he did not care at all.

Beyond the finish line, the whole group was waiting in a tangle of medals, foil blankets and wet faces, and they swallowed Sam in a hug that lifted him off the ground. Frank was already pouring tea from a flask the size of a fire extinguisher, Nadia was laughing and crying at once, and Maria simply held his hand and said nothing at all. It was, Sam thought, one of the finest minutes of his life, and he did not want it to end.

Afterwards, Ana sat with Sam on the grass and told him that the real finish line had been the day he first put on his shoes, and that every run from now on was a bonus. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor or physiotherapist who knows your own body and history. Run gently, listen carefully to yourself, and remember what Joy knew all along, which is that running should be a joy.
